paragraphs.text: A [rolled oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) grown in [Lugu](lugu:where-it-is), a mountain township of valleys and bamboo forest in the south west of Nantou County, in central Taiwan. Lugu is where [Dong Ding oolong](nantou:lugu-dong-ding) comes from. Its tea goes back to bushes [brought from Fujian](lugu:history) in the nineteenth century; the story told locally credits Lin Fengchi with a few seedlings planted on the slopes of Dong Ding. The township lies in the [middle belt](nantou:altitude-bands) of Nantou's tea country, below the high mountain gardens, where roasted oolong is at home.

This tea was made in 1996 and has had thirty years since, which places it in Taiwan's tradition of keeping oolong as [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea. Oolong kept this way is stored cool, dry, dark and sealed, and roasted again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in. No standard says how many years make an oolong old. Those who give a figure put it somewhere between ten and thirty, so at thirty years this tea sits at the far end of that count.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
